routes.description: Defend Christianity by connecting its account of sin and redemption to coherent explanations of suffering, divine judgment, biblical law, equality, and disputed Pauline instructions.
routes.successCriteria: Christianity's claims withstand the objections if its teachings on forgiveness and judgment remain morally coherent and the contested scriptural passages admit interpretations consistent with human dignity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account of salvation and divine goodness remains coherent across the principal moral and textual objections.

centralBridges.description: Explain how sin, Christ's sacrifice, forgiveness, judgment, and promised restoration form a coherent account of the human condition.
Reconcile divine jealousy, anger, and judgment with protective love, mercy, grace, and moral opposition to evil.
Interpret slavery regulations and restrictions on women without treating them as universal endorsements of ownership or subordination.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect disputed provisions to broader biblical themes of equal dignity, liberation, inclusion, and spiritual equality.
Use textual and congregational context to distinguish situational regulation from universal moral prescription.

routes.description: Challenge Christianity by presenting psychological alternatives to its consoling claims and testing divine goodness against troubling biblical portrayals, laws, and institutional restrictions.
routes.successCriteria: The skeptical critique satisfies its burden if central Christian defenses fail to reconcile the cited moral and textual difficulties with claims of divine goodness and scriptural authority.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cited Christian claims face unresolved explanatory, moral, or scriptural tensions substantial enough to defeat their proposed coherence.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Christianity's existential usefulness supplies a plausible psychological explanation distinct from the truth of its claims.
Test whether biblical portrayals of jealousy, violence, mutability, mercy, and love describe a morally consistent divine character.
Show that specific slavery provisions authorize ownership or coercion not explained merely as humane regulation of an existing practice.
Show that explicit Pauline restrictions create a moral problem not resolved by broader claims about Christian equality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use the rule separating a freed man from his family to test the claimed protective or transitional purpose of slavery legislation.
Test abolitionist use of spiritual-unity language against the parallel persistence of earthly male and female distinctions.

sectionSelections.title: Redemption, suffering, and explanatory origin
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue establishes Christianity's account of sin, forgiveness, suffering, judgment, and restoration while testing whether its existential appeal supports truth or an alternative psychological origin.

proSelections.proposition: Human sin brings separation from God, death, and hell, while Jesus's death offers grace, forgiveness, and eternal life to those who place faith in him.
The biblical worldview attributes suffering and injustice to human rebellion, presents God as entering suffering in Christ, and promises judgment, resurrection, and ultimate restoration.

conSelections.proposition: Christianity's capacity to overcome suffering and meaninglessness may indicate that people created it as an especially convenient source of spiritual consolation.

sectionSelections.title: Divine anger, love, and scriptural consistency
sectionSelections.rationale: The coherence of divine goodness depends on whether the Bible's depictions of jealousy, anger, violence, mercy, and love can describe one morally consistent divine character.

proSelections.proposition: God's jealousy and anger are righteous responses to evil and are consistent across the Testaments with divine mercy, grace, and judgment.

conSelections.proposition: The Old Testament's military, jealous, apparently vindictive, mutable, and localized portrayal of God appears difficult to reconcile with the portrayal associated with Jesus.

sectionSelections.title: Slavery law, regulation, and coercion
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether biblical slavery provisions merely constrain wrongdoing in a fallen society or instead authorize ownership and avoidable coercion contrary to divine justice.

proSelections.proposition: Old Testament slavery laws regulate conduct arising from hardened human hearts rather than endorse it, as Mosaic divorce rules permitted conduct contrary to God's original design.

conSelections.proposition: Biblical provisions permit purchasing foreigners as property and unequal treatment of slaves, appearing at least implicitly to condone ownership of human beings.
The regulation defense is challenged by a law that separates a freed man from his wife and children and thereby pressures him to accept lifelong slavery to remain with them.

sectionSelections.title: Canonical equality and earthly slavery
sectionSelections.rationale: The broader scriptural case against slavery turns on whether creation, liberation, inclusion, and unity in Christ condemn earthly slavery or describe equality compatible with continuing social distinctions.

proSelections.proposition: The wider biblical context opposes slavery through creation of all people in God's image, liberation from Egypt, Jesus's inclusion of Gentiles, and unity of slave and free in Christ.

conSelections.proposition: The statement that there is neither slave nor free cannot by itself establish earthly abolition because its parallel denial of male and female does not abolish earthly sex distinctions.

sectionSelections.title: Women teaching and speaking in church
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether New Testament evidence supports women's participation in teaching and worship or imposes a general rule of silence and subordination.

proSelections.proposition: Paul's approval of Priscilla teaching Apollos provides a New Testament example of a woman teaching a man.
Paul's instruction for women to remain silent addressed disorder in a particular congregation rather than imposing a universal ban, since women were permitted to pray and prophesy.

conSelections.proposition: First Corinthians 14 directs women to remain silent and subordinate in church and to ask their husbands at home, creating a New Testament moral problem.
